title: Does ICANN Open the Door on Identity Theft by Dropping 3rd Level .name Domains Registrations?
gist: ICANN approved Verisign's plan to discontinue third-level .name domain registrations (first.last.name), deleting ~22,000 legacy registrations after a 90-day notice and releasing their parent second-level domains for public re-registration, which security researchers warn creates a mass account-takeover and identity-theft vector.

insights.claim: The change stems from an ICANN Registry Services Evaluation Policy request submitted by registry operator Verisign on April 15, 2026, approved in late July 2026, under which Verisign is discontinuing third-level .name domain registrations (structured as first.last.name), citing declining usage and limited registrar support.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Establishes the precise regulatory timeline and rationale for anyone assessing legal or advocacy responses.
insights.locator: The move stems from an ICANN Registry Services

insights.claim: Operationally, EPP transactions will reject new third-level .name registrations going forward, and all existing active third-level registrations will be deleted following a minimum 90-day registrar notice period.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Gives affected registrants and downstream service providers a concrete compliance/migration deadline (90 days from registrar notice) to act before deletion.

insights.claim: The change does not decommission the entire .name TLD; Verisign will continue supporting standard second-level domain registrations (e.g., example.name), available since 2004, which remain unaffected.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Limits the scope of disruption to the legacy third-level naming scheme only, narrowing but not eliminating the affected population.
insights.locator: Importantly, the change does not decommission

insights.claim: The deletion of legacy third-level names directly impacts an estimated 22,000 registrants who adopted the structure when the .name TLD debuted in 2001 under Global Name Registry.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Quantifies the affected population for any legal, insurance, or breach-notification exposure calculus.
insights.locator: the complete deletion of legacy third-level names

insights.claim: Once third-level .name records are deleted, the parent second-level domains may become open for public registration, and a malicious actor acquiring a released second-level domain could configure DNS records to intercept communications, reset passwords, and hijack accounts tied to the legacy addresses.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Creates a systemic, low-cost account-takeover vector via password-reset flows and mail interception — any service that verified users via a .name third-level email address is now at long-tail risk once the second-level domain recycles.

insights.claim: Beyond identity theft, the deletion disrupts long-running websites, mail servers, and IoT infrastructure that depend on legacy third-level .name addresses.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: IoT and infrastructure dependent on ~25-year-old domain registrations is an underappreciated operational risk vector for anyone auditing legacy dependency chains.
insights.locator: Beyond the immediate disruption to long-running websites

insights.claim: Online technical communities on Hacker News and Mastodon characterized the likely fallout as 'identity theft-as-a-service,' warning that orphaned email addresses will become prime automated-takeover targets, and criticized Verisign's filing for claiming registrars identified no security, stability, or resiliency concerns.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Community consensus directly disputes the regulatory filing's own risk assessment, suggesting the approval process under-weighted security review — a governance failure pattern relevant to other TLD/registry policy changes.
insights.locator: Several observers characterised the resulting fallout

insights.claim: Engineers on Hacker News argued the decision sets a damaging precedent for registry stewardship and proposed that Verisign should either freeze existing delegations in perpetual read-only mode or permanently reserve the associated second-level domains rather than releasing them.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Offers a concrete alternative remediation (freeze/reserve) that affected registrants and advocacy groups could push ICANN/Verisign to adopt before deletion completes.
insights.locator: Engineers on Hacker News noted that the decision

insights.claim: Software engineer Neil Fraser, whose own .name domain (registered nearly 25 years ago) is scheduled for deletion, is exploring administrative appeals or legal challenges against ICANN and Verisign, framing himself as one of 22,000 people who will lose their domains.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A named, credible individual pursuing legal action could set precedent for how ICANN registry-service-evaluation approvals are challenged going forward.
insights.quote: I'm just one of 22,000 people who will lose their domains. This is going to be fun. Time to lawyer up...
